title: Critical path vs critical chain
blurb: Differentiate critical path from critical chain, and explain project buffers, feeding buffers and buffer management.
question: A pharmaceutical company's lab fit-out keeps slipping even though every task estimate includes generous safety time. One specialist engineer is needed on several tasks at once. A consultant recommends critical chain scheduling. How would it differ from the current critical path schedule, and why might it help?

teach.body: Critical path scheduling finds the longest sequence of dependent activities, assuming the resources will be there when needed. Critical chain scheduling is resource-constrained: it finds the longest chain of activities once BOTH the task logic and the availability of resources are taken into account. It also removes the safety margin hidden in each task and pools it into shared buffers. Plain English: critical path asks 'what order?', critical chain also asks 'who is free to do it?'

teach.h: Why safety time inside tasks gets wasted
teach.body: When every estimate is padded, the padding rarely protects the end date. Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time available, so a task given ten days takes ten days even if it could take seven. Student syndrome: people start late because the deadline feels comfortable, then hit a problem with no time left. Early finishes are seldom passed on, but late finishes always are. Critical chain tackles both behaviours.

teach.h: Traditional plan: safety hidden in every task
teach.caption: Illustrative. Each task carries its own safety time, which tends to be used up whether needed or not.

teach.h: Critical chain plan: safety pooled into buffers
teach.caption: Red bars are the critical chain. Safety removed from each task is pooled into a project buffer at the end; a feeding buffer sits where a non-critical chain joins the critical chain.

teach.body: On the critical path plan, 'Validate equipment' and 'Calibrate sensors' run in parallel, because the logic allows it. But both need Priya, the only validation engineer. She cannot do two jobs at once, so the plan was never achievable. Critical chain schedules around Priya: one task follows the other, and the chain now runs through her work. The resource dependency is made visible, and the buffers protect the date.

teach.h: Managing by buffer consumption: a typical approach
teach.caption: Each week compare buffer used with chain completed. Green: use is in line with progress. Amber: buffer is being used faster than the chain is progressing. Red: little buffer left, so act now.

teach.text: Don't swap the buffers. The PROJECT buffer sits at the END of the critical chain and protects the completion date. FEEDING buffers sit where a non-critical chain JOINS the critical chain, so delays on that feeder do not hold up the critical chain. And critical chain is not 'critical path with float renamed': it schedules around resources and pools safety.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Critical path: longest sequence of dependent activities, zero float, assumes resources are available.
Critical chain: resource-constrained, so the chain reflects resource dependencies as well as logic.
Safety margins are removed from individual tasks and pooled as buffers: a project buffer at the end, feeding buffers where non-critical chains join.
Progress is managed by buffer consumption rather than float on individual tasks.
Benefit: it reduces Parkinson's law and student syndrome, protecting the end date with less total safety time.
Critical path: logic-driven, resources assumed available, protected by float.
Critical chain: resource-constrained, safety pooled into buffers.
Project buffer at the end of the chain; feeding buffers where feeder chains join it.
Monitor buffer consumption against chain progress to know when to act.
Both are mainly linear-schedule techniques; iterative projects protect dates by fixing time boxes and flexing scope.

summary: You can now differentiate critical path from critical chain: one driven by activity logic with resources assumed available, the other constrained by resources with safety pooled into buffers. You can also place the project and feeding buffers correctly and explain why buffer consumption is what gets monitored.

A.q: What is the main distinguishing focus of critical chain scheduling compared with critical path?
options: Recording the cost of each activity
Removing all dependencies between tasks
Scheduling around resource availability
Adding extra float to every single task
A.why: Critical chain is resource-constrained: it builds the schedule around resource dependencies as well as task logic, whereas critical path assumes resources will be available.

whyNot.0: Cost recording belongs to cost control and earned value, not to the choice of scheduling technique.
whyNot.1: Dependencies remain; critical chain adds resource dependencies to the task logic.
whyNot.3: It does the opposite: it strips safety from tasks and pools it into buffers.

A.q: In a critical chain schedule, where is the project buffer placed?
options: At the end of the critical chain
At the start of every work package
Inside each critical activity estimate
Where a feeder chain joins the main chain
A.why: The project buffer sits at the end of the critical chain, just before the completion date, so it absorbs variation along the whole chain.

whyNot.1: Buffers are not placed at the start of work packages.
whyNot.2: Safety inside individual estimates is exactly what critical chain removes.
whyNot.3: That location is for a feeding buffer, not the project buffer.

A.q: What is the purpose of a feeding buffer in critical chain scheduling?
options: To fund extra staff when the chain runs late
To protect the chain from delays on feeder paths
To hold scope that was deferred by the client
To give each team member some personal slack
A.why: A feeding buffer is placed where a non-critical chain joins the critical chain, so that a delay on the feeder does not hold up the critical chain.

whyNot.0: Buffers are time, not money. Funding for known risks is contingency.
whyNot.2: Deferred scope is handled through change control or backlog prioritisation, not a buffer.
whyNot.3: Personal slack is the hidden padding critical chain removes.

B.q: Complete the statement: Parkinson's law suggests that work ______.
options: always finishes earlier than first estimated
expands to fill the time available for it
is best estimated by the most senior expert
should be split evenly across the whole team
B.why: Parkinson's law says work expands to fill the time available. Generous estimates therefore get used up, which is one reason critical chain removes padding from individual tasks.

whyNot.0: The point of Parkinson's law is the reverse: time saved is rarely handed back.
whyNot.2: This relates to estimating approaches, not Parkinson's law.
whyNot.3: Workload distribution is a resource question, unrelated to Parkinson's law.

B.q: A design team was given three weeks for a task. They start it in the final week and then discover a problem they cannot fix in time. Which behaviour does this illustrate?
options: Scope creep
Resource levelling
Student syndrome
Fast-tracking
B.why: Student syndrome is leaving work until the last moment because the deadline feels comfortable, so there is no time left when problems appear.

whyNot.0: Scope creep is uncontrolled growth in scope, not starting late.
whyNot.1: Levelling delays activities to fit resource limits; it is a planning technique, not a behaviour.
whyNot.3: Fast-tracking overlaps activities to save time; it does not describe a late start.

B.q: On a critical chain project, what is the main measure the project manager uses to judge whether the schedule is under control?
options: The number of milestones achieved
How much each task's padding was used
The total float left on every activity
Buffer used compared with chain completed
B.why: Critical chain is managed through buffer consumption: comparing how much buffer has been used with how much of the chain is complete shows whether action is needed.

whyNot.0: Milestones help, but the defining critical chain measure is buffer consumption.
whyNot.1: Individual task padding is removed, so there is none to measure.
whyNot.2: Float on each activity is the critical path way of tracking, not critical chain.

C.q: Two activities can run in parallel according to the logic, but both need the same specialist tester. How would a critical chain schedule treat them?
options: Keep them in parallel and add float to both
Sequence them so the chain runs through the tester
Remove one activity from the project scope
Move both activities into the project buffer
C.why: Critical chain recognises the resource dependency: one person cannot do both at once, so the activities are sequenced and the chain follows the constrained resource.

whyNot.0: Keeping them in parallel ignores the resource constraint, which is the critical path weakness.
whyNot.2: The work is still needed; the issue is sequencing, not scope.
whyNot.3: Buffers hold pooled safety time, not activities.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of critical chain scheduling?
options: It pools safety time into shared buffers
It places feeding buffers where chains join
It adds a safety margin to each single task
It tracks progress by buffer consumption
C.why: Critical chain removes safety margins from individual tasks. Adding padding to each task is the traditional approach it replaces.

whyNot.0: Pooling safety into buffers is the core idea of critical chain.
whyNot.1: Feeding buffers protect the critical chain where non-critical chains join it.
whyNot.3: Buffer consumption is how critical chain progress is monitored.

C.q: Halfway through a critical chain project, 70% of the project buffer has been used but only 30% of the chain is complete. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Take recovery action now and alert the sponsor
Do nothing, because buffer exists to be used up
Add the buffer back into each task's estimate
Wait until the buffer is fully used to report
C.why: Buffer is being consumed far faster than the chain is progressing, which is an early warning that the end date is at risk. The project manager should act and escalate now, while options remain.

whyNot.1: Buffer is meant to absorb variation, but the rate of use matters. Using it this fast signals a problem.
whyNot.2: Putting padding back into tasks reverses the method and invites Parkinson's law.
whyNot.3: Waiting removes the chance to recover; buffer monitoring exists to give early warning.

reteach.title: Think of planning a wedding day
reteach.question: Every supplier quotes a time with a cushion built in, and the one photographer is needed for both the bride's and the groom's photos. How would a critical chain planner run the day?

blocks.h: One shared cushion, not lots of little ones
blocks.body: If hair, flowers, cars and the photographer each add 20 spare minutes, the spare time quietly disappears: people relax because they 'have time'. A critical chain planner asks each supplier for a tight but realistic time and keeps one shared cushion just before the ceremony (the project buffer). The single photographer can't be in two places, so the groom's photos follow the bride's. The flowers are needed for the groom's photos, so a small cushion where that delivery joins (a feeding buffer) protects the main chain.

blocks.caption: Red is the critical chain, which runs through the photographer. Amber blocks are pooled safety: one at the end, one where the flowers join.

blocks.text: The big shared cushion sits at the END of the chain (project buffer). Small cushions sit where side jobs JOIN it (feeding buffers).

explain.body: Critical path analysis works out the longest path from activity logic and durations. It assumes the resources will be available when the logic says an activity can start. Where resources are scarce or shared, that assumption can make the plan unachievable.

explain.h: Logic says parallel; one engineer says no
explain.caption: The critical path plan runs both at once. With only one engineer, that plan cannot be delivered.

test.q: What assumption does traditional critical path analysis make about resources?
options: They will be available when needed
They must be shared across all tasks
They are scheduled before the logic
They are held in a separate buffer
test.why: Critical path analysis is driven by logic and durations and assumes resources will be there when activities are due to start. Critical chain drops that assumption.

whyNot.1: Critical path makes no assumption that resources are shared; it largely ignores resource limits.
whyNot.2: Critical path schedules from the logic; resources are considered afterwards, if at all.
whyNot.3: Buffers are a critical chain feature.

explain.body: Padding in every estimate tends to be consumed by Parkinson's law and student syndrome, and early finishes are rarely passed on. Critical chain uses aggressive but achievable estimates and moves the safety into shared buffers where it actually protects the date.

test.q: Why does critical chain take safety margins out of individual task estimates?
options: To cut the overall budget for the project
Because padded time tends to get used up
Because tasks are never late in practice
To remove the need to monitor progress
test.why: Safety held inside tasks is usually consumed by behaviours such as Parkinson's law and student syndrome. Pooling it into buffers makes it protect the end date instead.

whyNot.0: The aim is schedule protection, not a budget cut.
whyNot.2: Tasks are often late, which is why buffers are still needed.
whyNot.3: Progress is still monitored, through buffer consumption.

explain.body: The project buffer sits at the end of the critical chain and protects the completion date. Feeding buffers sit where non-critical chains join the critical chain, protecting it from delays on those feeders.

test.q: Which TWO are buffers used in critical chain scheduling? 1. Project buffer 2. Feeding buffer 3. Management reserve 4. Total float
options: 1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 2
test.why: Critical chain uses a project buffer at the end of the chain and feeding buffers where non-critical chains join it.

whyNot.0: Management reserve is money held for unknowns, not a critical chain time buffer.
whyNot.1: Total float is a critical path concept, not a buffer.
whyNot.2: Neither is a critical chain buffer: one is a cost reserve, the other a critical path measure.

explain.body: Critical path: logic first, resources assumed, float on non-critical activities, progress tracked by dates and float. Critical chain: resource-constrained, safety pooled into buffers, progress tracked by buffer consumption. Same goal, protecting the end date, different method.

test.q: A colleague says critical chain is just critical path with the float renamed as buffers. What is the best response?
options: Correct: the two methods produce identical plans
Correct: buffers are float moved to the start
No: critical chain ignores task logic entirely
No: it schedules around resources and pools safety
test.why: Critical chain differs in two ways: it accounts for resource constraints, and it removes safety from tasks and pools it into buffers that are actively managed.

whyNot.0: The plans differ, because resource dependencies change the sequence and buffers replace padding.
whyNot.1: Buffers are pooled safety, placed at the end and at join points, not float moved to the start.
whyNot.2: Critical chain still uses task logic; it adds resource dependencies to it.
